e.t: Abdenagō is a personal name, rendered “Abdenagō” or “Avthenago.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 11 times, all in Daniel, from Daniel 1:7 through Daniel 3:97. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly its role as a personal designation; the supplied material does not provide a separate word-definition or explanation of the name’s etymology.

This word means “holiness”: the quality or condition of being holy. It is a noun used to name holiness itself, and its rendering remains consistent across all five occurrences in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here. The word appears four times in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees, showing its use in language that speaks about what is holy. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes something that is “unfounded” or “unlawful”—without a valid basis or contrary to what is permitted. It can characterize an action, claim, or condition as lacking rightful support or violating an established rule. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something unjustified or forbidden.

Aitōb, also rendered Etov, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 11:11. The name identifies a person in that passage, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the details needed to understand that person’s role. Its meaning is therefore its identification as a proper name, not a general concept or instruction.

This Greek LXX noun means “shouting”: a forceful vocal cry expressed aloud. It names the act or sound of shouting rather than a person, place, or abstract idea. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including uses in Joshua, Psalms, Jeremiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This word means “carelessly,” describing an action done without sufficient attention, care, or concern. As an adverb, it explains how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is acting in a careless or heedless manner.

This adjective means “ambidextrous”: able to use either hand with comparable skill. It describes a person whose ability is not limited to one preferred hand. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Judges. The basic idea is a two-sided or both-handed ability, while the surrounding verse determines what person or action the adjective describes.

This Greek LXX verb means “draw up”: to pull or lift something upward. It describes upward movement rather than simply remaining in place, and its exact application depends on what is being drawn up in the sentence. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in Daniel, Amos, and Habakkuk. Its basic sense remains focused on bringing something from a lower position upward.

This adjective describes something that is out of reach or unattainable. It refers to what cannot be reached, obtained, or accomplished within the situation being described. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), in 3 Maccabees 2:15. Its basic sense remains focused on impossibility of attainment rather than on a particular emotion, event, or spiritual condition. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being called unattainable there.

This Greek LXX adjective means “unbearable,” describing something that cannot reasonably be endured or carried. It presents a situation, burden, or demand as too difficult to withstand. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Exodus 18:18, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: the matter in view is beyond what a person can continue bearing.

This noun means “meeting with”: it refers to coming together with another person or party. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 24 times across 23 verses, so it describes a recurring kind of meeting rather than a rare technical term. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on who is meeting and why, but the word itself centers on the meeting. It occurs in books from 2 Samuel through 2 Kings.

This LXX Greek verb means “take away” or “receive.” It describes an action in which something is taken, removed, or accepted, depending on the sentence. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including Numbers, Isaiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on what is being taken or received in that context.

This Greek LXX noun means “head” or “chief,” referring to one who stands foremost or leads others. Its basic sense can describe a person recognized as having prominence or authority. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 24:31. Since the word appears only there, its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Araouritēs is a proper name, appearing as “Araouritēs; Arauritis.” It identifies a particular person or group designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 23:33. Because the verse text and wider context are not included here, its precise referent in that passage cannot be described further; the secure meaning is its function as a name or designation.

Arēsa, also written “Arisa,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament record. This name occurs twice in the Septuagint, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. Because the available information gives the name but no surrounding verse text, it does not establish the person’s role, family, or significance. Those details must be understood from the passages where the name appears.

This word means “spice,” referring to an aromatic substance used for fragrance, flavor, or ceremonial purposes. It is a noun naming such materials rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, including passages involving stored spices, gifts, burial preparations, and fragrant imagery. Its precise use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an aromatic spice or mixture of spices.

Asaremoth is a noun preserved as a name-like term, with the gloss “Hasaremot?” indicating uncertainty about its precise identification. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Jeremiah 38:40. Since the available wording does not provide a broader definition or surrounding verse text, its ordinary meaning cannot be expanded beyond this proper-name rendering. The term is therefore best understood as an uncertain name or designation rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or general object.

Asrōni, also rendered Azroni, is a proper name used to identify a person or family group in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs twice, both times in Numbers 26, so its role is as a specific designation rather than a general description or action. The name is preserved as a name in English rather than translated into an ordinary meaning-word. Its precise reference in each occurrence depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an occupation or business—the work or activity with which a person is engaged. Its sense is practical and broad, naming what someone is occupied with rather than identifying a particular profession. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines the precise aspect of that occupation or business being discussed.

This verb means to spend the night, describing remaining somewhere through the nighttime rather than leaving immediately. It can refer simply to lodging or staying overnight, and its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 41 times, showing that this is a recurring word for overnight stay. The word is also used in passages translated from both historical and poetic portions of the Greek Old Testament.

This adjective describes something or someone as “without grace.” It expresses the absence of grace or graciousness, rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 20:19. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but its basic meaning remains a lack of grace. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

Baithsour, also rendered Vethsur, is a proper name for a place or locality in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary descriptive word or an action; it identifies a named location. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. The precise significance of the place in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its broader setting.

This word is a proper name rather than a general description. It is given in the forms “Baithchor” and “Vethkhor,” which identify the same named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 7:11. Without the verse text, its specific reference cannot be described further here, but its basic function is to name rather than express an action, quality, or general idea.

This word is a proper name for a place called “Bērōtha” or “Virotha.” It is not presented as a common description or action, but as the name of a specific location in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Ezekiel 47:16, and its precise significance there depends on the surrounding passage and the geographical setting described by Ezekiel. The name itself identifies the place rather than expressing a general quality, event, or spiritual concept.

Gabee, also rendered Gavee, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs seven times in this LXX corpus, in seven verses, with occurrences in 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular referent cannot be stated safely.

This noun refers to soothsayers—people regarded as able to reveal hidden knowledge or predict events through divination. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Daniel, where it is used as a recognized category of specialists consulted for mysterious matters. The word identifies a type of person rather than describing a specific prediction or method. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means a “spear” or “javelin,” referring to a weapon used in battle. It is a noun naming the weapon itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Joshua 8:18. Its appearance there places it among military equipment, while its basic meaning remains straightforward: a spear-like weapon used for combat. The precise force of the word in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun describes arrogance or exultation—a proud sense of superiority or joyful triumph. Its meaning can point either to boastful self-importance or to an elevated, celebrating spirit, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Job and twice in Sirach. Because the individual verse texts are not provided here, the precise emphasis in each occurrence cannot be stated, but the central idea remains a heightened attitude expressed through pride or exultation.

This adjective describes something ridiculous or absurd—something that appears plainly foolish, unreasonable, or worthy of scorn. It is a descriptive word, used to characterize a person’s words, reasoning, or action rather than name a separate object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what the surrounding sentence identifies as foolish or unreasonable.

This verb means “tithe”: to give a tenth as an offering. It describes the act of setting apart and presenting one-tenth of something, especially in worship or support of God’s appointed service. As a verb, it expresses what a person does rather than naming the offering itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:38, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the available verse text does not provide further context.

This noun refers to one of the people—a commoner rather than someone identified by rank or special status. It describes a person as belonging to the ordinary population. In the Greek of the Septuagint’s deuterocanonical books, it occurs once, at Wisdom 18:11. That single occurrence confirms its basic social meaning, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain the word’s particular force there. Its central idea is an ordinary member of the people.

This Greek LXX verb means “arouse” or “rouse”—to awaken, stir, or prompt someone or something into activity. It describes an action that brings a person or thing out of inactivity and into alertness or movement. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Esther, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being aroused and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “handful,” referring to an amount that can be held in one hand. It describes a small, measurable quantity rather than an abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: twice in Old Testament books and once in 3 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense remains consistent across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines what material or thing is being held.

This Greek LXX noun means “consecration” or “dedication”: the setting apart of something for a sacred purpose. It names the act or occasion of dedicating something to God, rather than describing a person, object, or feeling by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 7:88. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the formal dedication of something for holy use.

Eleasa is a proper name rendered “Eleasa.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in Old Testament verses. The available references are in 1 Chronicles and Jeremiah, but verse text is not included, so those references do not establish additional meaning beyond its role as a proper name.

Elisaph is a personal name, also rendered Elisaf. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears seven times, chiefly in Numbers and once in Ezra. The available wording establishes the person’s name, but not its deeper name meaning or the individual details of each occurrence. Its precise significance in any passage must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

gl: next to; in the presence of
d: next to; in the presence of

e.t: This word means “next to” or “in the presence of.” It functions as an adverb or preposition, indicating that someone or something is nearby, alongside another, or before another person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 250 times, showing regular use for describing position or proximity. Its exact English wording may depend on the sentence, but its central idea remains being beside or in front of someone or something.

This Greek LXX verb means “present” or “set in.” It describes something as having arrived or now being present, and it functions as an action word rather than a name or description. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what has become present or what has set in there.

This verb means “strive for” or “search for”—to actively seek something, pursue it, or look for it. In the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, it can describe purposeful seeking rather than a merely casual glance. Its 16 occurrences span the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so the basic idea is broad enough to cover both searching for a person or thing and earnestly pursuing a desired outcome. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is most natural.

This Greek LXX verb means “consider,” describing the act of giving something thoughtful attention. It points to deliberate reflection rather than a passing glance or immediate reaction. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 1:30. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise emphasis in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself; its basic sense remains thoughtful consideration.

This noun means “staying on” or “tarrying”—remaining in a place or continuing rather than departing. It describes continued presence or delay, and its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding context. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 38:27. The word therefore points to the act or condition of remaining, lingering, or continuing in place, rather than to a person, object, or separate action. Its meaning is concise: persistence in staying or a period of waiting.

“Ermōniim; Ermonim” is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a particular place or geographic feature in the Greek Old Testament wording. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Psalms 41:7. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise identification and significance in that passage cannot be explained further from the word alone.

This word means “well” or “rightly,” expressing approval or affirming that something is done correctly. It can function as an adverb, describing the manner of an action, or as an interjection expressing a response such as approval. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times across nine verses, including passages in Job, Psalms, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a positive acknowledgment that something is good, proper, or rightly done.

This adjective describes someone or something with a white speck on it. It refers to a visible white marking or spot, rather than expressing an action or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 21:20. Because it is an adjective, its role is to describe a person or thing by this outward feature. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its list of described conditions.

Thale is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:25. Because the available lexical meaning is simply the name itself and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its personal identity and role must be understood from that passage’s context. The name is therefore best read as a recorded personal designation, not as a word with a broader ordinary definition.

Thersa is a proper name, used as a name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore centered on the named subject in each passage, and the surrounding verse identifies which mention is intended. In the Greek Old Testament, Thersa occurs 15 times in 13 verses, appearing from Numbers through 2 Kings. The name is rendered consistently as “Thersa.”

This adverb means “fiercely.” It describes an action done with intense, wild, or forceful energy, rather than calmly or gently. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 12:15. The word itself tells how an action is carried out; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the action and explain its particular force there. It is therefore a manner word, modifying the event or behavior being described.

Iakaba, also rendered Iakava, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Septuagint text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:36. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is its identifying function: it distinguishes the individual named in that genealogy or list. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role there.

This word is a proper name rendered as “Iessiou” or “Iessiu.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Samuel 14:49 and once in 2 Chronicles 26:22. The name’s precise identity and role depend on the surrounding passage, since the word itself functions simply as a personal designation.

gl: one who comes to seek protection; suppliant
d: one who comes to seek protection; suppliant

e.t: This Greek Old Testament noun means “one who comes to seek protection; suppliant”—a person who approaches another for refuge, help, or favor. It describes someone appealing for protection rather than acting as a self-sufficient authority. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including Psalms, Malachi, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on whom the suppliant approaches and what protection or appeal the surrounding text describes.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iōada” or “Ioatha.” It identifies a person by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah: once in Nehemiah 12:22 and again in Nehemiah 13:28. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about the person or the role being described.

Ioasar is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 2:18. The available lexical information preserves the name as “Iōasar” or “Ioasar,” but does not provide a further definition or explain the name’s meaning. Its precise identification and significance in that genealogy depend on the surrounding passage and the people listed there.

Iōzabad, also rendered Iozavath, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears seven times in this LXX corpus, including passages in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Ezra. Its exact significance for any one occurrence must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This word refers to a gecko, also described as a spotted lizard. It is a noun naming a small crawling creature rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Leviticus and once in Proverbs. Those references show that the word belongs to ordinary animal vocabulary, while the exact significance of either passage depends on the verse and its surrounding text. Its central meaning remains the creature itself: a gecko or spotted lizard.

gl: hearten; ravish the heart of sb
d: hearten; ravish the heart of sb

e.t: This verb means to “hearten” someone or to “ravish the heart of someone.” It describes an action that strongly affects another person’s inner feelings, either by strengthening the heart or deeply captivating it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Song of Songs 4:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a powerful effect on another person’s heart.

This verb means “break,” describing the act of causing something to split, crack, or be broken. It presents breaking as an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Samuel and Zechariah. The exact object being broken and the force or purpose of the action must be understood from the surrounding verse, since the word itself gives the basic action but not every detail of the situation.

This verb means to accomplish something—to bring it about or carry it through—and can also describe cultivating or developing something. It focuses on purposeful action that produces a result. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, so its precise emphasis depends on whether the passage concerns completing a task or tending something so it can grow and become fruitful. The word appears from Exodus through Ezekiel and is used in varied settings, while retaining this central idea of actively bringing about an intended outcome.

This Greek LXX word means “lowest,” describing something at the bottom or in the least elevated position. It can function as an adjective, identifying what is lowest, and its use may also be treated as a noun when referring to the lowest place or position itself. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Nehemiah, Psalms, and Lamentations. Its clearest repeated rendering is “lowest,” especially in three Psalm passages. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to physical position, rank, or another form of low placement.

This noun means “heir”: a person entitled to receive what is passed down from another. It describes someone connected to an inheritance or succession, whether the word refers to one heir or several. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from Judges, 2 Samuel, Jeremiah, Micah, and Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Koulon, also rendered Kulon, is a proper name for a place. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographic name preserved in the Greek Septuagint. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:59. Without the verse text or surrounding passage, its precise location and role in that passage cannot be explained further here.

This adjective means “dog-like,” describing something associated with or resembling a dog. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 25:3. The word itself gives a basic comparison, but the precise force of that comparison in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, whose text is not included here. Its meaning is therefore best kept to the stated sense: dog-like, functioning as an adjective that describes a person or thing.

This word describes something curved or arched rather than straight. It can function as an adjective, identifying a bent shape, or as a noun referring to something with that shape. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Leviticus 21:20 and 1 Kings 21:11. Its basic meaning remains physical and descriptive; the surrounding verse determines exactly what curved or arched object is being mentioned.

This Greek Old Testament adjective means “mute” or “dull.” It can describe someone unable to speak, and it can also describe a lack of responsiveness or sharpness. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Psalms, Isaiah, Habakkuk, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force depends on what it describes in a sentence: a person, a bodily ability, or a condition marked by dullness. The basic idea remains an absence of normal speech or perceptive responsiveness.

This verb means “mix with frankincense.” It describes adding or combining something with frankincense, the fragrant substance used in biblical worship and offerings. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 3 Maccabees 5:45. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its ordinary lexical sense is clear: something is prepared or treated by being mixed with frankincense.

This Greek LXX verb means “winnow” or “drive away.” It describes an action of separating or removing, with the specific emphasis determined by the surrounding sentence. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Amos 9:9. Its basic sense remains focused on moving something away or separating it, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in Amos 9:9 must be understood from that passage’s immediate context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “especially,” marking one person, thing, or point as more notable or important than others in the sentence. It adds emphasis rather than naming an object or action by itself. The word appears six times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, across 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what it is emphasizing, but its central idea remains focused distinction: something is especially prominent, preferred, or noteworthy.

Machabēna, also rendered Makhavina, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 2:49. The available wording identifies the name itself, but the reference alone does not establish whether it belongs to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise identification therefore depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This adjective describes someone who boasts or talks big—using proud, exaggerated, or self-important speech. It points to a manner of speaking marked by confidence that goes beyond humility or restraint. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, once in Psalms and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning is clear: boastful speech or a boastful speaker.

This Greek LXX noun means a part or portion of something, and can also identify one particular section or share. It describes something considered as belonging to a larger whole rather than the whole itself. The word occurs 124 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic idea applies in contexts involving divisions, portions, or distinct parts. The precise sense in any verse depends on what larger whole is being divided or singled out.

This word means “only” or “alone.” It marks something as exclusive, limited to one person or thing, or occurring without others. As an adjective or adverb, it can describe who is present, what is included, or the narrow extent of an action or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 57 times, with both senses appearing across the collection. Its basic force is to set something apart from all others or to emphasize that nothing else is included.

Mola is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:33. Its meaning is therefore primarily identifying: it names Mola rather than expressing a general idea. The available lexical information does not provide a broader descriptive definition. The precise referent of the name belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, while the word itself functions as a preserved name in the Greek text.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Mōrēd” or “Morith.” It is not a common noun describing an object, action, or quality, so its meaning is primarily the identification of that individual. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:18. The precise significance of the person named there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a personal name rather than as a general descriptive term.

Naphag, also rendered Nafag, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: once in 1 Chronicles 3:7 and again in 1 Chronicles 14:6. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning for a reader is primarily the identification of a particular person; the surrounding verse is needed to determine which person is meant in each occurrence.

This word refers to a falcon, a bird of prey. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, where its precise role depends on the surrounding passage. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 39:13. Because the available lexical definition is specific, its central meaning is simply the bird itself rather than an abstract quality, action, or title.

This Greek LXX verb means “destroy” or “make an end of,” describing the ending or ruin of something. It is an action word rather than a name or description, and its sense centers on bringing something to its conclusion through destruction. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 23 times in 21 verses, including passages in Job, Proverbs, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what person or thing is being described as destroyed.

This Greek LXX noun means “disgrace”: a condition of dishonor, shame, or public reproach. It describes the loss of respect or dignity that brings shame upon a person or people. The word occurs 47 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so it expresses a recurring biblical idea rather than a rare or specialized term. Its exact force—whether personal shame, social dishonor, or reproach directed against a community—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Orpha, also written Orfa, is a personal name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies the Moabite woman who married one of Naomi’s sons. The name occurs twice, both times in Ruth: once in Ruth 1:4 and again in Ruth 1:14. Its meaning as a personal name is simply the woman’s designation in the narrative; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain her specific actions or role in either occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “scent” or “odour”—a smell that can be perceived. It names the fragrance or odor itself rather than an action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Hosea 14:7. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context, but its ordinary meaning remains a smell or fragrance that can be noticed.

This verb means “discipline.” It describes the action of disciplining someone, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, it occurs 81 times, showing that it is a recurring action-word across the collection. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of discipline.

This verb means “compared” or “like,” expressing the act of setting something alongside another thing to show a likeness or correspondence. It describes comparison rather than simply naming an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both in Psalm 48, so its broader range cannot be established from many examples. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and sentence. [p03:word:lxx:L710106:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710106:occurrences]

This noun means “father’s brother; uncle,” referring to a man related through one’s father. It identifies a specific family relationship rather than a general male relative. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four Old Testament verses, showing a precise and limited family term. English translations commonly render it as “uncle,” while the fuller definition makes clear that the relationship is specifically the father’s brother. The exact reference of the word in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to something made ripe or ready by the sun—literally, something “cooked by the sun; ripe.” It describes fruit or produce that has reached maturity through exposure to the sun, rather than something still unready. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Numbers 11:5, so its precise force there belongs to the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning is the condition of being naturally ripened or softened by the sun.

This Greek LXX verb means “plate with silver,” describing the act of covering or furnishing an object with a silver surface. It is used mainly in descriptions of the tabernacle and its furnishings, where materials and craftsmanship are carefully specified. The word occurs nine times across eight Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, including passages in Exodus, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the object being described, but its central idea remains applying silver as an outer covering or finish.

This verb means to wrap something around oneself or to gird up, especially by securing clothing around the body. It describes an action that prepares a person for movement, work, travel, or another task. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 35 times, chiefly in passages from the Old Testament portion of the Septuagint, with two occurrences in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being wrapped or what activity the person is preparing to undertake.

This verb expresses believing someone or something and, in a stronger relational sense, entrusting oneself or something to another. It can describe confident acceptance or placing trust, while the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on belief or entrustment. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 78 times, showing a recurring word for responding with trust. Its basic meaning is therefore active reliance, not merely awareness or intellectual agreement.

Wordiness means using more words than are needed. This noun names speech characterized by an excess of words, drawing attention to how much is said rather than simply to the content. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 10:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the presence or use of many words.

This adjective means “wordy,” describing speech or expression that uses many words. It identifies a quality of someone’s speaking or wording rather than naming an action, object, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 8:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a description of excessive or lengthy speech. The word therefore points readers to how much is being said, not necessarily to whether the words are true or false.

This verb expresses the act of “despatch besides”—sending someone or something additionally, alongside what has already been sent or arranged. It presents an added dispatch rather than a standalone action, so its basic sense includes the idea of sending further. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 11:14. The verse text is not included, so the precise person or purpose of that additional dispatch cannot be stated from the word alone.

The word means “confirm possession”: it describes the act of establishing or affirming that something is possessed or belongs to someone. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 10:39. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly how that confirmation functions there.

This verb means “stitch together”: it describes joining separate pieces by stitching them into one. Its basic sense focuses on the action of bringing parts together rather than on the finished object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, so its meaning is established through a small number of uses rather than a wide range of repeated appearances. The surrounding wording determines what is being joined in any particular verse.

Sarbacha, also rendered Sarvakha, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. As a proper noun in the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person. It occurs once in the Septuagint, in Esther 9:8. The available lexical information establishes the name itself, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

Selmōn, also rendered Selmon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person or place named Selmon, though the available information does not specify which in each occurrence. It appears twice in this corpus: once in 2 Samuel 23:28 and once in Psalm 67:15. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the particular referent and significance of each occurrence must be determined from its context.

Sephela is a proper name, also rendered Sefila, rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies the named subject wherever it occurs in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. This name appears five times in the Greek LXX corpus: four times in Old Testament books and once in 1 Maccabees. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This Greek verb means to “stir up” or “hoe,” describing the action of agitating or working the soil. It can therefore refer to turning something over, disturbing it, or cultivating it, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 76:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise force in that occurrence cannot be stated beyond these established meanings.

Souia, also rendered Soia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or named group in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Ezra 2:43 and once in Nehemiah 7:47. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity cannot be clarified further, but its basic function is simply to serve as a personal designation.

This noun means “relatives,” referring to people connected by family ties or shared ancestry. It describes kin as a group rather than one individual family member. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 36 times, showing a recurring way to speak about family connections across genealogies, households, and the wider community. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains people joined by familial relationship.

This noun means false accusation or oppression: wrongdoing that unjustly charges, pressures, or crushes another person. It can describe deceptive accusation as well as harsh treatment that places someone under unjust power. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, including three occurrences in Ecclesiastes, where oppression is repeatedly identified as a serious human evil. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “sing with”: it describes joining another person or group in singing rather than singing alone. As a verb, it expresses the action of participating in shared song. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both within one verse in Hosea. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific scene, but the word itself centers on singing together or accompanying others in song.

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to “head off with” or “lead off with,” describing the act of departing while taking someone or something along. It is an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 14:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is movement accompanied by what is being led or taken.

This verb means to hide something together with something else. It describes concealed items sharing the same hiding place or being hidden alongside another thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:48. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be stated beyond this basic action. Its central idea remains concealment in company with something else.

This Greek LXX verb means “coordinate; arrange.” It describes putting people, things, or actions into an ordered relationship or sequence. As a verb, it expresses the act of organizing rather than the arrangement itself. It occurs 112 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing a recurring word for ordering or coordinating. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being arranged and the surrounding passage.

This word means “cord,” referring to a length of material used as a line or fastening. It is a noun, so it names the physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 27 times across 27 verses, showing repeated use for a tangible cord in different passages. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Sōphar, also rendered Sofar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a personal name in the Greek Old Testament and appears nine times, from Genesis through Job. Its occurrence in Job is especially frequent, but the name itself does not provide a broader definition or spiritual meaning apart from identifying the person or named individual in its context.

This word means “ashes,” the powdery remains left after something has been burned. It is a noun naming that material rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 2:3. That single occurrence establishes its ordinary lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain any specific comparison or message attached to ashes there. The word therefore refers plainly to the residue of fire or burning.

This adjective describes someone or something “commanding under”—exercising command while remaining under a higher authority. It points to a subordinate place within an order of command rather than independent rule. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages from Genesis, Job, Lamentations, Habakkuk, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the person or thing being described.

This Greek Old Testament noun refers to something made by weaving, especially a woven robe or a web. It is used for a crafted textile in descriptions of priestly garments, and for a web in the account involving Samson. The word occurs six times across the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Judges, and Job. Its central idea is a woven structure or fabric, with the exact object identified by the surrounding passage.

Pharsannestain is a proper name, functioning as an identifying personal name rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. The Greek Old Testament form appears once, in Esther 9:7. It is represented by the name “Pharsannestain,” with “Farsannesten” also given as a spelling variant. Since no broader usage is recorded, its precise referent must be understood from the surrounding passage.

Chaldaisti is an adverb meaning “Chaldaisti,” identifying speech or expression as Chaldean. It describes how something is said rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:26. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic function is to mark the language or manner of expression as Chaldean.

“Chalphi” or “Khalfi” is a personal name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:70. The name’s particular referent cannot be identified from the lexical information alone because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here. Its ordinary function is simply to identify an individual.

Chanani, also rendered Khanani, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in Ezra 9:1 and Nehemiah 9:4. Since no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name itself establishes identity, while the passages supply the details about the person and role. Its meaning as a personal name should therefore not be expanded into an additional description or spiritual concept.

This Greek LXX verb means “joke.” It describes the act of joking or making a remark in a joking manner, rather than naming a person, object, or abstract quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, each in a different deuterocanonical book. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

Chorri, also rendered Khorri, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with a separate action, quality, or concept; its meaning is the personal name itself. The name occurs six times in six Old Testament verses, appearing in Genesis, 2 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise identification in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This adverb means “heartily” or “from the heart,” describing an action done with sincere inner commitment rather than merely outwardly. It tells how someone acts or responds, emphasizing wholehearted feeling or willingness. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains action that comes genuinely from within.

Ōdouia, also given as “Othoia,” is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies people in genealogical and community lists. It occurs five times, from 1 Chronicles through Ezra and Nehemiah, so its role is to name individuals, while the surrounding verse determines which individual is meant. The name itself is not assigned a further definition here.

This word is a proper name, referring to Ōreb, also rendered Oriv. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs five times across three verses, appearing four times in Judges and once in Psalms. Its exact significance in any one passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.
